newsitem.title: USA: CompUSA reports weak Christmas sales, stock drops.
newsitem.headline: CompUSA reports weak Christmas sales, stock drops.

text.p: CompUSA Inc., one of the strongest computer retailers, Thursday blamed weak holiday sales of personal computers for a disappointingly small rise in sales in the last three months of 1996.

Chief Executive Officer James Halpin said sales growth had been fairly solid but suddenly softened in the last two weeks of December. The company said that sales from stores open at last a year, or same-store sales, rose 1.5 percent in the last three months of 1996.

Most industry analysts had expected CompUSA's sales for the three months ended Dec. 28 to rise about 3 percent, and the company's stock dropped $4.625, about 22 percent, to $16 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Halpin said in an interview he was "not happy" with the downturn in consumer sales but said other computer retailers were suffering even more and that CompUSA would continue to gain market share.

Best Buy Co. Inc. last month reported its first quarterly loss in more than a decade and Tandy Corp. this week said it was selling its chain of Incredible Universe superstores and shutting down 19 of its 108 Computer City stores in North America.

CompUSA's poor retail sales performance in the last three months underlined the mounting evidence of a sharp slide in the growth of personal computer sales because the Dallas-based company had consistently bettered market expectations over the last two years.
Goldman Sachs responded by cutting its rating on CompUSA to "market perform" from "outperform".
Halpin said he thought holiday sales were slow because many customers preferred to wait for the introduction next week of Intel's new multimedia MMX chip before upgrading their computers.

"We think our corporate customers and a lot of our retail customers are waiting for that chip to come out on Jan. 8," Halpin said, playing down concerns that the MMX technology might not have attracted sufficient publicity to drive a new wave of computer upgrades.
"The technical people, the corporate customers and heavy computer users certainly understand it," he said.
Halpin said CompUSA's growth in other areas such as service business and direct sales to corporations was helping it survive the slowdown in the retail business.
"While I'm not happy with sales, I am certainly pleased with the way our business continues to run."
CompUSA's overall sales for the last three months of 1996 were $1.2 billion, up 22 percent from $983 million in the year-ago period.
Analysts said CompUSA was in a better position than most of its competitors but that the sector might continue to suffer in coming months.

"The environment is going to be very difficult. You are going to continue to have lower-than-normal growth and that is going to make it more competitive," said George Sutton, an analyst with Rauscher Pierce Refsnes.
The short-term future for computer retailers appears now to depend on the response to the new MMX multimedia chips.

Sutton said many retailers had shed excess inventory ahead of the launch. "Certainly, the retail perspective is that it could be something that is a requirement on a newly-purchased computer. Whether that drives demand or not is hard to say but it is something retailers are preparing for."
